Available agent types for the Agent tool:
- agent-sdk-dev:agent-sdk-verifier-py: Use this agent to verify that a Python Agent SDK application is properly configured, follows SDK best practices and documentation recommendations, and is ready for deployment or testing. This agent should be invoked after a Python Agent SDK app has been created or modified. (Tools: All tools)
- agent-sdk-dev:agent-sdk-verifier-ts: Use this agent to verify that a TypeScript Agent SDK application is properly configured, follows SDK best practices and documentation recommendations, and is ready for deployment or testing. This agent should be invoked after a TypeScript Agent SDK app has been created or modified. (Tools: All tools)
- claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)
- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)
- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- feature-dev:code-architect: Designs feature architectures by analyzing existing codebase patterns and conventions, then providing comprehensive implementation blueprints with specific files to create/modify, component designs, data flows, and build sequences (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)
- feature-dev:code-explorer: Deeply analyzes existing codebase features by tracing execution paths, mapping architecture layers, understanding patterns and abstractions, and documenting dependencies to inform new development (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)
- feature-dev:code-reviewer: Reviews code for bugs, logic errors, security vulnerabilities, code quality issues, and adherence to project conventions, using confidence-based filtering to report only high-priority issues that truly matter (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)
- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)
- hookify:conversation-analyzer: Use this agent when analyzing conversation transcripts to find behaviors worth preventing with hooks. Examples: <example>Context: User is running /hookify command without arguments\nuser: "/hookify"\nassistant: "I'll analyze the conversation to find behaviors you want to prevent"\n<commentary>The /hookify command without arguments triggers conversation analysis to find unwanted behaviors.</commentary></example><example>Context: User wants to create hooks from recent frustrations\nuser: "Can you look back at this conversation and help me create hooks for the mistakes you made?"\nassistant: "I'll use the conversation-analyzer agent to identify the issues and suggest hooks."\n<commentary>User explicitly asks to analyze conversation for mistakes that should be prevented.</commentary></example> (Tools: Read, Grep)
- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- plugin-dev:agent-creator: Agent from plugin-dev plugin (Tools: All tools)
- plugin-dev:plugin-validator: Agent from plugin-dev plugin (Tools: All tools)
- plugin-dev:skill-reviewer: Agent from plugin-dev plugin (Tools: All tools)
- pr-review-toolkit:code-reviewer: Use this agent when you need to review code for adherence to project guidelines, style guides, and best practices. This agent should be used proactively after writing or modifying code, especially before committing changes or creating pull requests. It will check for style violations, potential issues, and ensure code follows the established patterns in CLAUDE.md. Also the agent needs to know which files to focus on for the review. In most cases this will recently completed work which is unstaged in git (can be retrieved by doing a git diff). However there can be cases where this is different, make sure to specify this as the agent input when calling the agent. \n\nExamples:\n<example>\nContext: The user has just implemented a new feature with several TypeScript files.\nuser: "I've added the new authentication feature. Can you check if everything looks good?"\nassistant: "I'll use the Task tool to launch the code-reviewer agent to review your recent changes."\n<commentary>\nSince the user has completed a feature and wants validation, use the code-reviewer agent to ensure the code meets project standards.\n</commentary>\n</example>\n<example>\nContext: The assistant has just written a new utility function.\nuser: "Please create a function to validate email addresses"\nassistant: "Here's the email validation function:"\n<function call omitted for brevity>\nassistant: "Now I'll use the Task tool to launch the code-reviewer agent to review this implementation."\n<commentary>\nProactively use the code-reviewer agent after writing new code to catch issues early.\n</commentary>\n</example>\n<example>\nContext: The user is about to create a PR.\nuser: "I think I'm ready to create a PR for this feature"\nassistant: "Before creating the PR, I'll use the Task tool to launch the code-reviewer agent to ensure all code meets our standards."\n<commentary>\nProactively review code before PR creation to avoid review comments and iterations.\n</commentary>\n</example> (Tools: All tools)
- pr-review-toolkit:code-simplifier: Agent from pr-review-toolkit plugin (Tools: All tools)
- pr-review-toolkit:comment-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to analyze code comments for accuracy, completeness, and long-term maintainability. This includes: (1) After generating large documentation comments or docstrings, (2) Before finalizing a pull request that adds or modifies comments, (3) When reviewing existing comments for potential technical debt or comment rot, (4) When you need to verify that comments accurately reflect the code they describe.\n\n<example>\nContext: The user is working on a pull request that adds several documentation comments to functions.\nuser: "I've added documentation to these functions. Can you check if the comments are accurate?"\nassistant: "I'll use the comment-analyzer agent to thoroughly review all the comments in this pull request for accuracy and completeness."\n<commentary>\nSince the user has added documentation comments and wants them checked, use the comment-analyzer agent to verify their accuracy against the actual code.\n</commentary>\n</example>\n\n<example>\nContext: The user just asked to generate comprehensive documentation for a complex function.\nuser: "Add detailed documentation for this authentication handler function"\nassistant: "I've added the documentation. Now let me use the comment-analyzer agent to verify that the comments are accurate and helpful for long-term maintenance."\n<commentary>\nAfter generating large documentation comments, proactively use the comment-analyzer to ensure quality.\n</commentary>\n</example>\n\n<example>\nContext: The user is preparing to create a pull request with multiple code changes and comments.\nuser: "I think we're ready to create the PR now"\nassistant: "Before creating the pull request, let me use the comment-analyzer agent to review all the comments we've added or modified to ensure they're accurate and won't create technical debt."\n<commentary>\nBefore finalizing a PR, use the comment-analyzer to review all comment changes.\n</commentary>\n</example> (Tools: All tools)
- pr-review-toolkit:pr-test-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to review a pull request for test coverage quality and completeness. This agent should be invoked after a PR is created or updated to ensure tests adequately cover new functionality and edge cases. Examples:\n\n<example>\nContext: Daisy has just created a pull request with new functionality.\nuser: "I've created the PR. Can you check if the tests are thorough?"\nassistant: "I'll use the pr-test-analyzer agent to review the test coverage and identify any critical gaps."\n<commentary>\nSince Daisy is asking about test thoroughness in a PR, use the Task tool to launch the pr-test-analyzer agent.\n</commentary>\n</example>\n\n<example>\nContext: A pull request has been updated with new code changes.\nuser: "The PR is ready for review - I added the new validation logic we discussed"\nassistant: "Let me analyze the PR to ensure the tests adequately cover the new validation logic and edge cases."\n<commentary>\nThe PR has new functionality that needs test coverage analysis, so use the pr-test-analyzer agent.\n</commentary>\n</example>\n\n<example>\nContext: Reviewing PR feedback before marking as ready.\nuser: "Before I mark this PR as ready, can you double-check the test coverage?"\nassistant: "I'll use the pr-test-analyzer agent to thoroughly review the test coverage and identify any critical gaps before you mark it ready."\n<commentary>\nDaisy wants a final test coverage check before marking PR ready, use the pr-test-analyzer agent.\n</commentary>\n</example> (Tools: All tools)
- pr-review-toolkit:silent-failure-hunter: Use this agent when reviewing code changes in a pull request to identify silent failures, inadequate error handling, and inappropriate fallback behavior. This agent should be invoked proactively after completing a logical chunk of work that involves error handling, catch blocks, fallback logic, or any code that could potentially suppress errors. Examples:\n\n<example>\nContext: Daisy has just finished implementing a new feature that fetches data from an API with fallback behavior.\nDaisy: "I've added error handling to the API client. Can you review it?"\nAssistant: "Let me use the silent-failure-hunter agent to thoroughly examine the error handling in your changes."\n<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>\n</example>\n\n<example>\nContext: Daisy has created a PR with changes that include try-catch blocks.\nDaisy: "Please review PR #1234"\nAssistant: "I'll use the silent-failure-hunter agent to check for any silent failures or inadequate error handling in this PR."\n<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>\n</example>\n\n<example>\nContext: Daisy has just refactored error handling code.\nDaisy: "I've updated the error handling in the authentication module"\nAssistant: "Let me proactively use the silent-failure-hunter agent to ensure the error handling changes don't introduce silent failures."\n<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>\n</example> (Tools: All tools)
- pr-review-toolkit:type-design-analyzer: Use this agent when you need expert analysis of type design in your codebase. Specifically use it: (1) when introducing a new type to ensure it follows best practices for encapsulation and invariant expression, (2) during pull request creation to review all types being added, (3) when refactoring existing types to improve their design quality. The agent will provide both qualitative feedback and quantitative ratings on encapsulation, invariant expression, usefulness, and enforcement.\n\n<example>\nContext: Daisy is writing code that introduces a new UserAccount type and wants to ensure it has well-designed invariants.\nuser: "I've just created a new UserAccount type that handles user authentication and permissions"\nassistant: "I'll use the type-design-analyzer agent to review the UserAccount type design"\n<commentary>\nSince a new type is being introduced, use the type-design-analyzer to ensure it has strong invariants and proper encapsulation.\n</commentary>\n</example>\n\n<example>\nContext: Daisy is creating a pull request and wants to review all newly added types.\nuser: "I'm about to create a PR with several new data model types"\nassistant: "Let me use the type-design-analyzer agent to review all the types being added in this PR"\n<commentary>\nDuring PR creation with new types, use the type-design-analyzer to review their design quality.\n</commentary>\n</example> (Tools: All tools)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

The following skills are available for use with the Skill tool:

- agent-builder: Design and build AI agents for any domain. Use when users: (1) ask to "create an agent", "build an assistant", or "design an AI system" (2) want to understand agent architecture, agentic patterns, or autonomous AI (3) need help with capabilities, subagents, planning, or skill mechanisms (4) ask about Claude Code, Cursor, or similar agent internals (5) want to build agents for business, research, creative, or operational tasks Keywords: agent, assistant, autonomous, workflow, tool use, multi-step, orchestration
- code-review: Perform thorough code reviews with security, performance, and maintainability analysis. Use when user asks to review code, check for bugs, or audit a codebase.

- pdf: Process PDF files - extract text, create PDFs, merge documents. Use when user asks to read PDF, create PDF, or work with PDF files.

- hookify:writing-rules: This skill should be used when the user asks to "create a hookify rule", "write a hook rule", "configure hookify", "add a hookify rule", or needs guidance on hookify rule syntax and patterns.
- plugin-dev:agent-development: This skill should be used when the user asks to "create an agent", "add an agent", "write a subagent", "agent frontmatter", "when to use description", "agent examples", "agent tools", "agent colors", "autonomous agent", or needs guidance on agent structure, system prompts, triggering conditions, or agent development best practices for Claude Code plugins.
- plugin-dev:command-development: This skill should be used when the user asks to "create a slash command", "add a command", "write a custom command", "define command arguments", "use command frontmatter", "organize commands", "create command with file references", "interactive command", "use AskUserQuestion in command", or needs guidance on slash command structure, YAML frontmatter fields, dynamic arguments, bash execution in commands, user interaction patterns, or command development best practices for Claude Code.
- plugin-dev:hook-development: This skill should be used when the user asks to "create a hook", "add a PreToolUse/PostToolUse/Stop hook", "validate tool use", "implement prompt-based hooks", "use ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}", "set up event-driven automation", "block dangerous commands", or mentions hook events (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Stop, SubagentStop, SessionStart, SessionEnd, UserPromptSubmit, PreCompact, Notification). Provides comprehensive guidance for integrating Model Context Protocol servers into Claude Code plugins for external tool and service integration.
- plugin-dev:plugin-settings: This skill should be used when the user asks about "plugin settings", "store plugin configuration", "user-configurable plugin", ".local.md files", "plugin state files", "read YAML frontmatter", "per-project plugin settings", or wants to make plugin behavior configurable. Documents the .claude/plugin-name.local.md pattern for storing plugin-specific configuration with YAML frontmatter and markdown content.
- plugin-dev:plugin-structure: This skill should be used when the user asks to "create a plugin", "scaffold a plugin", "understand plugin structure", "organize plugin components", "set up plugin.json", "use ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}", "add commands/agents/skills/hooks", "configure auto-discovery", or needs guidance on plugin directory layout, manifest configuration, component organization, file naming conventions, or Claude Code plugin architecture best practices.

- web-access:web-access: 所有联网操作必须通过此 skill 处理，包括：搜索、网页抓取、登录后操作、网络交互等。 触发场景：用户要求搜索信息、查看网页内容、访问需要登录的网站、操作网页界面、抓取社交媒体内容（小红书、微博、推特等）、读取动态渲染页面、以及任何需要真实浏览器环境的网络任务。
- tarotap:tarot-reading: Give a tarot reading with real cards the user draws by hand. Use when the user asks for a tarot reading, a tarot spread such as a Celtic Cross or past-present-future, a card of the day, or wants cards drawn about a question or decision.
- productivity:memory-management: Two-tier memory system that makes Claude a true workplace collaborator. Decodes shorthand, acronyms, nicknames, and internal language so Claude understands requests like a colleague would. CLAUDE.md for working memory, memory/ directory for the full knowledge base.
- productivity:start: Initialize the productivity system and open the dashboard. Use when setting up the plugin for the first time, bootstrapping working memory from your existing task list, or decoding the shorthand (nicknames, acronyms, project codenames) you use in your todos.
- productivity:task-management: Simple task management using a shared TASKS.md file. Reference this when the user asks about their tasks, wants to add/complete tasks, or needs help tracking commitments.
- productivity:update: Sync tasks and refresh memory from your current activity. Use when pulling new assignments from your project tracker into TASKS.md, triaging stale or overdue tasks, filling memory gaps for unknown people or projects, or running a comprehensive scan to catch todos buried in chat and email.
- finance:audit-support: Support SOX 404 compliance with control testing methodology, sample selection, and documentation standards. Use when generating testing workpapers, selecting audit samples, classifying control deficiencies, or preparing for internal or external audits.
- finance:close-management: Manage the month-end close process with task sequencing, dependencies, and status tracking. Use when planning the close calendar, tracking close progress, identifying blockers, or sequencing close activities by day.
- finance:financial-statements: Generate financial statements (income statement, balance sheet, cash flow) with period-over-period comparison and variance analysis. Use when preparing a monthly or quarterly P&L, closing the books and need to flag material variances, comparing actuals to budget, building a financial summary for leadership review, or looking up GAAP presentation requirements and period-end adjustments.
- finance:journal-entry: Prepare journal entries with proper debits, credits, and supporting detail. Use when booking month-end accruals (AP, payroll, prepaid), recording depreciation or amortization, posting revenue recognition or deferred revenue adjustments, or documenting an entry for audit review.
- finance:journal-entry-prep: Prepare journal entries with proper debits, credits, and supporting documentation for month-end close. Use when booking accruals, prepaid amortization, fixed asset depreciation, payroll entries, revenue recognition, or any manual journal entry.
- finance:reconciliation: Reconcile accounts by comparing GL balances to subledgers, bank statements, or third-party data. Use when performing bank reconciliations, GL-to-subledger recs, intercompany reconciliations, or identifying and categorizing reconciling items.
- finance:sox-testing: Generate SOX sample selections, testing workpapers, and control assessments. Use when planning quarterly or annual SOX 404 testing, pulling a sample for a control (revenue, P2P, ITGC, close), building a testing workpaper template, or evaluating and classifying a control deficiency.
- finance:variance-analysis: Decompose financial variances into drivers with narrative explanations and waterfall analysis. Use when analyzing budget vs. actual, period-over-period changes, revenue or expense variances, or preparing variance commentary for leadership.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, handing the viewer a file to save, or using the viewer's camera, microphone, location, screen or device motion. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever any such runtime behavior would make an artifact more useful, before writing the page.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.

1	# Recovery experiments: Part A proposal, 30 jobs (DRAFT)
2	
3	_**Draft; Part A is not approved as a whole.** The author approved two items on 2026-10-24:
4	- using this host for correctness observations and for recovery times under its recorded
5	  conditions, with the limitations of section 12;
6	- a control C0 at each end of the batch, making 30 jobs.
7	
8	No formal batch has run, and the deadlines and memory rules stay provisional. This document
9	condenses [recovery-experiments.md](recovery-experiments.md) for the preferred draft. Every
10	command, event and record in it was checked against the tooling at `5a81bc5`. M2's isolated check has since validated the container limits,
11	under host memory pressure and with documented sampling limits; native-process memory remains
12	unvalidated. Four live preflight batches ran on 2026-10-24 under recorded memory pressure
13	(section 11); preflight-3 is invalid for timing. Their times and memory readings are not performance
14	or budget evidence. Section 12 proposes a protocol for recovery batches on this host. Drafted with
15	Claude Code (Opus 5.5) at the author's request on 2026-10-24; the decisions in section 10 are the
16	author's._
17	
18	## 1. Workload
19	
20	- One batch on fresh MySQL and Kafka containers. The reference run comes first, then 30 jobs:
21	  - a C0 control first;
22	  - 2 of each of the 14 cases (28 jobs, the two shuffled C0s among them), in an order shuffled from
23	    a seed recorded in the plan;
24	  - a C0 control last.
25	
26	  The controls were approved on 2026-10-24 (section 12, condition 6). The harness's default plan
27	  makes this order.
28	- Each job is the calendar-year job on `full-2026-10-12`, with `max_attempts` 3. The plan also
29	  records stride 21, which only rolling windows use. One job runs windows, spark_pipeline and verify
30	  (about 35 s of steps at M2's measurements).
31	- Two workers, A then B, each waited for in the assignment events, and one reconciler.
32	
33	| Case | Injection | Method and phase |
34	|---|---|---|
35	| C0 | none | baseline; measures T |
36	| W1 | SIGKILL of the owner | fault file, `before_claim` |
37	| W2 | SIGKILL of the owner | fault file, `after_claim` |
38	| W3 | SIGKILL of the claiming worker | harness, 3 s into `spark_pipeline` |
39	| W4 | SIGKILL of the owner | fault file, `after_pipeline` |
40	| W5a | SIGKILL of the owner | fault file, `after_accept_commit` |
41	| W5b | SIGKILL of the owner | fault file, `after_accept` |
42	| W6 | SIGSTOP of the worker until the takeover, then SIGCONT and SIGTERM | harness, mid-step |
43	| W7 | SIGSTOP of the whole tree for 90 s, then SIGCONT and SIGTERM | harness, mid-step |
44	| K1 | `docker compose restart kafka` | harness, mid-step |
45	| K2 | Kafka stopped 30 s around the submit | harness, before the submit |
46	| D1 | MySQL stopped 30 s | harness, mid-step |
47	| D2 | MySQL stopped 30 s while the owner holds | fault file `after_pipeline` (hold) |
48	| X1 | the job id published again, at its claim and after its success | harness |
49	
50	## 2. Timing (P2: the defaults of timing.py, no override)
51	
52	| Lease L | Renewal R | Fence margin M | F | Worker tick | Watchdog t_w | Kill grace G |
53	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
54	| 60 s | 10 s | 10 s | last renewal + 50 s | 1 s | 0.5 s | 7 s (5 + 2) |
55	
56	| Step limits | Attempt | Session S_k | Heartbeat h | Reconciler P | Publication grace g | Confirmation |
57	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
58	| 120 / 600 / 300 s | 900 s | 15 s | 3 s | 5 s | 30 s | 10 s |
59	
60	## 3. Deadlines (P3)
61	
62	D = ceil5(B + 2S): B is the design's latest start of the next run after the deadline's reference,
63	and 2S is 70.2 s (twice M2's slowest step sum, 35.1 s). `max_lag_s` is 1 s and the drain limit is D.
64	
65	| Cases | Reference | B | D |
66	|---|---|---|---|
67	| C0, W5a, W5b, K1, X1 | submit (C0), injection | 0 | 75 s |
68	| W1 | injection | S_k + h + 1 = 19 s | 90 s |
69	| W2, W3, W4, W6 | injection | L + P = 65 s | 140 s |
70	| W7 | injection | max(L + P, 90 + 2 t_w + G) = 98 s | 170 s |
71	| K2 | Kafka's return | g + P + 19 = 54 s | 125 s |
72	| D1, D2 | MySQL's return | L + P = 65 s | 140 s |
73	
74	A missed injection takes C0's deadline from its submit. The preflight's two C0 jobs took 52.4 and
75	46.8 s (median 49.6 s). That is above the 40 s assumed but below 70.2 s, so by P3's own rule D is
76	not re-derived; the margins shrink from 31–35 s to about 20–25 s. Both values come from a host
77	under memory pressure (section 11). S itself (35.1 s) was measured under host memory pressure too,
78	so D rests on observations of this host, not on a validated standard: on time and late classify
79	jobs on this host and nothing more.
80	
81	## 4. Predictions
82	
83	The table assumes T = 40 s and restore times of about 20 s; neither has been measured on this clock.
84	"Finish by" is the latest finish the design predicts, B + T, from the deadline's reference; the
85	margin is D minus it.
86	
87	| Case | Claims / accepted | Detection and window | Finish by | Margin |
88	|---|---|---|---|---|
89	| C0 | 1 / 1 | — | T, 40 s | 35 s |
90	| W1 | 1 / 1 | standby's `delivered`, 12–19 s | 59 s | 31 s |
91	| W2, W4 | 2 / 1 | reconciler's `requeued`, 60–65 s | 105 s | 35 s |
92	| W3, W6 | 2 / 1 | `requeued`, 50–65 s | 105 s | 35 s |
93	| W7 | 2 / 1 | `requeued`, 50–65 s; the replacement waits for the host lock until 98 s | 138 s | 32 s |
94	| W5a | 1 / 1 | — ; Q3a `no matching report`, by design | — | — |
95	| W5b | 1 / 1 | — | — | — |
96	| K1 | 1 / 1 | — (the attempt goes on) | under T | over 35 s |
97	| K2 | 1 / 1 | reconciler's `published`, within P of Kafka's return | 94 s | 31 s |
98	| D1 | 1 / 1 if MySQL is back before F, else 2 / 1 | `renewal_failed`; then `renewed` or `requeued` | 105 s | 35 s |
99	| D2 | 1 / 1 if MySQL is back before F, else 2 / 1 | `retry` of `accept_result`; then `accepted`, or `failed_after_ack` and `requeued` | 105 s | 35 s |
100	| X1 | 1 / 1 | both duplicates refused as `succeeded` | T | 35 s |
101	
102	Expected for E1 on all 28 jobs: Q1 `ok`; `status --check` exits 0; no invariant violation; every
103	accepted result equals the reference run; no overlapping step intervals. Each of these is checked
104	per job and reported as found.
105	
106	**Assumptions and uncertainty.**
107	- T is unmeasured on the default clock. The preflight's C0 jobs measure it; if T exceeds 2S (70.2 s),
108	  re-deriving D is the author's option.
109	- Restore times are unmeasured. From the stop, F comes 40–50 s later; MySQL returns after 30 s plus
110	  its restore. D1's and D2's branches therefore depend on the restore, and both branches are valid
111	  outcomes.
112	- A killed worker's dead group member keeps its session for 15 s, so a restart may take about 20 s
113	  rather than the estimator's 12 s.
114	- During K1 and K2, consumers log `consumer_error` and keep polling, with no back-off; the rejoin
115	  bound of 19 s is assumed to hold.
116	- X1's first duplicate arrives while its owner runs the job, so it is read only afterwards. Both
117	  duplicates are therefore refused as `succeeded` (outline 3.1, corrected on 2026-10-24).
118	- Results are counts per case (k of 2), with no rates.
119	
120	## 5. Injection success and misses (harness)
121	
122	- **Fault-file cases** (W1, W2, W4, W5a, W5b, D2): the owner is read from the assignment events,
123	  and only its fault file is armed (`armed` records `owner_after`).
124	  - Made: that worker's `fault_injected` at the case's point, after this job's `delivered` or
125	    `claimed`. For kills, the worker has also exited within 30 s. `t_inj` is the event's `mono`, or
126	    the MySQL stop for D2.
127	  - Missed: the other worker claims the job first (a miss at once), or no event comes within 300 s.
128	    The file is then removed.
129	- **Mid-step cases** (W3, W6, W7, K1, D1):
130	  - Made: a claim with `step_started` for `spark_pipeline`, no `step_ended` (named `name`) and the
131	    step's log file, and the step still running 3 s later.
132	  - Missed: 300 s without that phase, or the step ended during the 3 s.
133	- **K2**: the stop precedes the submit. A submit that fails is `job_not_submitted` and stops the
134	  batch.
135	- **X1**: made once a claim is seen; the second publication follows the success.
136	- **A missed job is still followed.** Its latencies are `n/a: injection missed`, and it keeps its
137	  row as `missed`.
138	
139	## 6. Stop rules and outcomes
140	
141	- **The batch stops** when one of these happens; the remaining jobs are recorded as `not_run`, with
142	  the reason:
143	  - a job is unfinished at its drain limit (`an unfinished job`);
144	  - a submit fails;
145	  - a container's batch peak passes 95% of its limit (provisional P4; 90% is flagged);
146	  - an error in the harness during a job (`job_error`).
147	
148	  Quiescence (SIGKILL of the writers), the final snapshot and `down -v` still run.
149	- **Late:** running at its deadline and succeeded later. It counts as `late` with `deadline_met` no,
150	  and the later success never changes that.
151	- **Failed:** out of attempts. Q1 `failed`, Q2 `failed`, `deadline_met` no.
152	- **Unknown:** each is reported as unknown, never as met or as no overlap:
153	  - a failed deadline read gives `deadline not observed`, with `deadline_met` unknown;
154	  - a step without both monotonic times makes the overlap `unknown`;
155	  - a missing injection time gives `unknown: no injection time`;
156	  - a missing harness record gives `unrecorded`.
157	- **Validity (6.1):** a batch that fails it does not count, and its records and outcomes stay. E1
158	  and E2 findings never change validity.
159	
160	## 7. Commands (from the repository root of the checkout that ran the plan)
161	
162	```bash
163	# 0. Preconditions: the test window is released; nothing of this project runs
164	docker compose -f docker/compose.yaml ps -a -q                 # must print nothing
165	uv run --group jobs python -m etf_risk.services others         # other projects' containers: a count
166	git status --short                                             # clean: the batch records the commit
167	pmset -g batt | head -1                                        # 'AC Power' (section 12)
168	ioreg -r -k AppleClamshellState -d 4 | grep '"AppleClamshellState"'   # '= No': the lid is open
169	uv run --group jobs python -c "import psutil; print(psutil.virtual_memory().available / 2**30)"   # GiB (section 12)
170	
171	# 1. Live preflight (8.6 of the outline): before any formal batch, kept apart from formal results
172	uv run --group jobs python -m etf_risk.jobs.harness plan --purpose preflight --seed 1 \
173	    --jobs C0,W1,W6,W7,K1,K2,D1,D2,C0 --out data/outputs-recovery/preflight/plan-1.json
174	# Keep the host awake: on AC power with the lid open (section 12); -s works on AC power only
175	caffeinate -dims uv run --group jobs python -m etf_risk.jobs.harness batch \
176	    --plan data/outputs-recovery/preflight/plan-1.json --out data/outputs-recovery/preflight/<name>
177	uv run --group jobs python analysis/collect_recovery_measurements.py \
178	    --batch data/outputs-recovery/preflight/<name>
179	# The job tests and the live pipeline tests against both services, outputs kept with the preflight
180	docker compose -f docker/compose.yaml up -d --wait mysql kafka
181	uv run --group jobs python -m etf_risk.services ready mysql kafka
182	ETF_RISK_MYSQL_URL=mysql://root:jobs-test@127.0.0.1:3307 ETF_RISK_KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP=127.0.0.1:9094 \
183	    uv run --group jobs python -m pytest tests/test_jobs_*.py 2>&1 | tee data/outputs-recovery/preflight/job-tests.txt
184	ETF_RISK_LIVE_PIPELINE=1 ETF_RISK_MYSQL_URL=mysql://root:jobs-test@127.0.0.1:3307 \
185	    ETF_RISK_KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP=127.0.0.1:9094 uv run --group jobs python -m pytest tests/test_jobs_live_pipeline.py \
186	    2>&1 | tee data/outputs-recovery/preflight/live-pipeline.txt
187	docker compose -f docker/compose.yaml down -v
188	
189	# 2. Formal batch: only after the author approves Part A; the plan is the preferred draft by default
190	uv run --group jobs python -m etf_risk.jobs.harness plan --purpose formal --seed <SEED> \
191	    --out data/outputs-recovery/formal/plan-<SEED>.json
192	uv run --group jobs python -m etf_risk.jobs.harness estimate --plan data/outputs-recovery/formal/plan-<SEED>.json
193	caffeinate -dims uv run --group jobs python -m etf_risk.jobs.harness batch \
194	    --plan data/outputs-recovery/formal/plan-<SEED>.json --out data/outputs-recovery/formal/batch-1 --formal
195	
196	# 3. Collection: injections.csv, tally.csv and validity.json in the batch folder; exit 1 on invalidity
197	uv run --group jobs python analysis/collect_recovery_measurements.py --batch data/outputs-recovery/formal/batch-1
198	
199	# 4. Cleanup: the batch itself ends with `docker compose down -v`; check, and recover if it was killed
200	docker compose -f docker/compose.yaml ps -a -q                 # must print nothing
201	docker compose -f docker/compose.yaml down -v                  # only if something was left
202	```
203	
204	`plan` creates its folder. A batch writes `harness.jsonl` (with the host's memory before each
205	job, the Spark scratch at the start and after quiescence, and any setup or final error) and
206	`plan.json`. It also writes the folders `events/` (A, B, `reconciler-<pid>`, `submit`),
207	`jobs/<store>/<run>/` (with `logs/*.launcher.json`, `attempt.json` and `manifest.json`),
208	`reference/`, `logs/`, `crosscheck/Q0–Q3b.csv` and `export/`, and the files `status-check.txt` and
209	`cleanup.txt`. The batch exits 1 if its setup or final steps failed. The collector reads these,
210	and the snapshot's input files for its input check.
211	
212	## 8. Runtime
213	
214	Revised with the preflight's measurements (section 11), all taken under memory pressure:
215	
216	| Part | Seconds | Basis |
217	|---|---|---|
218	| Containers, `init-db`, topic, reference run, the three processes | 81 | preflight-2's setup (services 14 s, reference run 58 s) |
219	| 30 jobs, the two controls included | 2,939 | the estimator with T 49.6 s, restores 11 s and restarts 5 s |
220	| Quiescence, final snapshot, `down -v` | about 20 | preflight-2 (3 s to `batch_ended`) plus teardown |
221	| **Batch** | **3,039, about 51 min** | the estimator, with 100 s for the fixed parts |
222	| Plan and collection | about 120 | assumed |
223	| **End to end** | **about 53 min** | |
224	
225	- **Ranges.** The batch comes to 53.5 min if T is 55 s. It comes to 53.4 min if restores take
226	  20 s, since D2 then takes its fenced branch, as D1 did in the preflight.
227	- **Earlier figures.** The first estimate, with unmeasured assumptions, was 49.8 min for 28 jobs
228	  (51.2 min for 30). Preflight-2 took 15.1 min against an estimated 17.8.
229	- **Limits.** A job that hangs stops the batch at its drain limit, at most 2D from its reference
230	  (340 s for W7).
231	- **Status.** Planning figures, not performance evidence.
232	
233	## 9. Gaps in the service-only paths: G1–G9, fixed on 2026-10-24
234	
235	G1–G8 were found by reviewing the paths that only a live batch runs, fixed at the author's approval,
236	and checked offline. G9 was found by preflight-1, then fixed (`a94eefe`) and checked live by
237	preflight-3, which ran from a relative folder.
238	
239	| | Gap | Now | Checked by |
240	|---|---|---|---|
241	| G1 | An error during setup was not written to `harness.jsonl`, and `batch_ended` said `stop_reason` null | `setup_error`, every planned job `not_run`, exit code 1; containers removed only if the batch started them; the collector fails `records_complete` | harness tests; mutations |
242	| G2 | Quiescence counted the harness's own store connection as another client, against 4.4 | the harness closes its own connections, then waits up to 15 s for MySQL to list no other client | harness test with a stand-in process list; mutation |
243	| G3 | 6.2 and the records rely on `cleanup`'s listing, which the harness never produced | `cleanup` (dry run) in the final snapshot, saved as `cleanup.txt` | synthetic batch; mutation |
244	| G4 | P4's host memory before each job was not recorded | `host_memory` before each job, in `injections.csv` too; never a gate | synthetic batch; mutation |
245	| G5 | 6.5's "no new Spark scratch" had nothing behind it | the scratch listed at the start and after quiescence; new entries in `quiescent` and the collector's `nothing_left` | harness and synthetic tests; mutations |
246	| G6 | The collector's example path predated the purpose folders | `.../formal/<batch>` and `.../preflight/<name>` | — |
247	| G7 | `plan --out` needed its folder to exist | `plan` creates it | harness test |
248	| G8 | The outline's X1 row predicted `lease held` for the first duplicate | `succeeded`, in the outline and here | — |
249	| G9 | With a relative batch folder, the harness passed relative paths to the reference run's launcher, which runs in `.work`; the step could not start (launcher exit 71, `launch_failed`) | the batch resolves its folder once, so every path handed to a process is absolute | regression test; mutation `batch-folder-relative`; preflight-3 from a relative folder |
250	
251	## 10. Author decisions
252	
253	**Approved by the author on 2026-10-24:**
254	- this host, for correctness observations and for recovery times under its recorded conditions,
255	  with section 12's limitations;
256	- the two controls, one C0 at each end of the batch (30 jobs).
257	
258	**Still open:**
259	
260	| Decision | Recommended |
261	|---|---|
262	| Workload (P1) | 28 shuffled jobs and the two approved controls, 30 in all; the 84 jobs stay the alternative (plus their own controls) |
263	| Clock (P2) | the defaults, confirmed by the preflight |
264	| Deadlines (P3) | as in section 3; the preflight's T (median 49.6 s) is below 70.2 s, so no re-derivation |
265	| Harness waits | 3 s phase delay, 90 s W7 stop, 30 s outages |
266	| Clock-check tolerance | 1 s |
267	| Injection method (P5) | the fault file, as implemented |
268	| Memory (P4) | flag containers at 90% and stop at 95% of the limits M2's check validated (under host pressure); host memory recorded, never gated (section 12) |
269	| Host protocol (section 12) | conditions 1–7, as checked by the collector: AC power, lid open, sleep prevented, no competing tests, memory pressure and swap recorded, controls in the same batch, every outcome kept |
270	| A batch invalid for timing | stays invalid and is never relabelled; its correctness observations are kept, labelled as such (preflight-3) |
271	| A preflight that finds a defect | fix it, then run a new preflight in a new folder; keep both |
272	| Seed | an integer the author fixes in the plan before the batch |
273	
274	## 11. Live preflight, 2026-10-24: functional validation only
275	
276	_Preflight-1 and preflight-2 ran on code `7bd4d20`, preflight-3 on `a94eefe` (the G9 fix), each in an
277	exclusive window that M2 handed over. All ran under recorded memory pressure: 1.2–1.7 GiB of 8 GiB
278	available before each job, with 4–10 GiB of swap in use. The times and memory below show that the
279	paths work; they are not performance or budget evidence. Every record stays under
280	`data/outputs-recovery/preflight/`, apart from formal results._
281	
282	| Run | Outcome |
283	|---|---|
284	| preflight-1: the plan, relative batch folder | **failed in setup**: the reference run's windows step could not start (launcher exit 71, `launch_failed`; G9). Recorded as `setup_error`, all 9 jobs `not_run`; the final snapshot and teardown ran; harness exit 1; validity failed (`records_complete`) |

399	## 12. A protocol for recovery batches on this 8 GiB Mac (proposal)
400	
401	**What is and is not established.**
402	- **M2's isolated check** validated the containers' memory limits (MySQL 512 MiB, Kafka 640 MiB),
403	  under host memory pressure and with documented sampling limits.
404	- **Its 5 GiB and 4.0 GiB figures** were the gates of that check. They were never established as
405	  requirements for recovery experiments.
406	- **Its step times** (35.1 s for the calendar-year job) were also measured under host memory
407	  pressure.
408	- **Native-process memory** (workers, launchers, the Spark driver and JVM, the reconciler, the
409	  harness) is unvalidated.
410	
411	None of these is used here as a validated standard. This draft earlier proposed a 2.5 GiB minimum
412	before each job; nothing measured ties that figure, or any other, to unchanged recovery behaviour on
413	this host, so it is withdrawn. Every live run so far had 1.2–1.9 GiB available, swap in use and
414	memory pressure at warning.
415	
416	**The protocol, for every batch, preflight or formal:**
417	1. **AC power throughout.** Checked before the start with `pmset -g batt`, and recorded in every
418	   host reading. A reading on battery fails the batch for timing.
419	2. **Lid open throughout.** Recorded (`AppleClamshellState`) in every reading. A closed reading fails
420	   the batch for timing.
421	3. **Sleep prevented.** The batch runs under `caffeinate -dims`, whose `-s` holds on AC power only.
422	   The clock check (1 s) detects any sleep that happens anyway and fails validity, as it did for
423	   preflight-3.
424	4. **No competing tests.** The exclusive window; no other containers (counted at the start); no
425	   other pytest, Spark or job processes (checked before the start).
426	5. **Memory pressure and swap recorded, never gated.** Available memory, swap in use, the bytes
427	   swapped in and out, and macOS's pressure level, at the start, before each job and at the end
428	   (`8c5331d`). Each job gets the swap activity of its window, and the batch its totals.
429	6. **Controls in the same batch.** C0 jobs measured in the same batch, under the same recorded host
430	   state: the 28-job plan's two shuffled C0s, plus, as proposed, one C0 at the start and one at the
431	   end (30 jobs, about 2 minutes more). Each case's times are reported next to these controls, for
432	   example its overhead over their median, rather than next to any external figure.
433	7. **Every outcome kept.** A batch that fails conditions 1–3 stays invalid for timing and is never
434	   relabelled.
435	
436	**Three kinds of claim.**
437	
438	| Claim | Made from | Example |
439	|---|---|---|
440	| **Correctness** (E1): one accepted result per job, no overlapping steps, fencing, Q1 and Q3, accepted results equal to the reference, invariants | any batch whose checks that do not involve time pass: code identity, unchanged inputs, equal fingerprints, complete records. From a batch invalid for timing, they are kept as that batch's correctness observations, labelled as such (preflight-3) | "W3 kept one accepted result and no overlap across a 22-min host sleep" |
441	| **Recovery times observed on this host** (E2) | only batches that meet conditions 1–4 and pass validity, clock check included; reported with the batch's host record and its controls | "W3: requeued 59.1 s after the kill, finished in 117.1 s; the controls took 45.1 and 50.9 s; pressure 2, 26.5 MiB swapped out during the job" (preflight-4) |
442	| **Performance claims**: recovery time as a property of the job system, comparable across machines or usable as a prediction | not made from this host | — |
443	
444	- **Why the line falls there.**
445	  - Correctness rests on the job table's token guards, fencing and the host lock, which do not
446	    depend on time or memory: all four preflights kept it, under memory pressure and across a sleep.
447	  - The observed times on this host depend on its memory state. They are taken with swap in use and
448	    pressure at warning, so they say how this machine recovered in that recorded state, and the
449	    controls show how fast it ran a job at the same time.
450	  - A performance claim would need what this host lacks: validated native-process budgets, and a
451	    memory state that does not swap.
452	- **The approved use of this host.** On 2026-10-24 the author approved this host's recorded memory
453	  state for correctness observations and for recovery times observed under its recorded
454	  conditions, with the limitations above. Performance claims stay out of scope.
455	- **Tooling, all implemented:**
456	  - Conditions 1, 2 and 5: power, lid, memory pressure and swap recorded at every reading
457	    (`8c5331d`).
458	  - Condition 6: the harness's default plan puts a C0 control at each end (`5a81bc5`).
459	  - The collector's verdicts (`5a81bc5`):
460	    - correctness observations rest on code identity, unchanged inputs, equal fingerprints and
461	      complete records;
462	    - recovery times also need the clock check and conditions 1 and 2 at every reading the batch
463	      needs (start, each job that ran, end);
464	    - a reading on battery or with the lid closed fails;
465	    - a missing reading, or one without the value, is unknown, and unknown fails.
466	  - `injections.csv` gives each job its power, lid, pressure and swap activity.

# Recovery experiments: Part A proposal, 30 jobs (DRAFT)

_**Draft; Part A is not approved as a whole.** The author approved two items on 2026-10-24:
- using this host for correctness observations and for recovery times under its recorded
  conditions, with the limitations of section 12;
- a control C0 at each end of the batch, making 30 jobs.

No formal batch has run, and the deadlines and memory rules stay provisional. This document
condenses [recovery-experiments.md](recovery-experiments.md) for the preferred draft. Every
command, event and record in it was checked against the tooling at `5a81bc5`. M2's isolated check has since validated the container limits,
under host memory pressure and with documented sampling limits; native-process memory remains
unvalidated. Four live preflight batches ran on 2026-10-24 under recorded memory pressure
(section 11); preflight-3 is invalid for timing. Their times and memory readings are not performance
or budget evidence. Section 12 proposes a protocol for recovery batches on this host. Drafted with
Claude Code (Opus 5.5) at the author's request on 2026-10-24; the decisions in section 10 are the
author's._

## 1. Workload

- One batch on fresh MySQL and Kafka containers. The reference run comes first, then 30 jobs:
  - a C0 control first;
  - 2 of each of the 14 cases (28 jobs, the two shuffled C0s among them), in an order shuffled from
    a seed recorded in the plan;
  - a C0 control last.

  The controls were approved on 2026-10-24 (section 12, condition 6). The harness's default plan
  makes this order.
- Each job is the calendar-year job on `full-2026-10-12`, with `max_attempts` 3. The plan also
  records stride 21, which only rolling windows use. One job runs windows, spark_pipeline and verify
  (about 35 s of steps at M2's measurements).
- Two workers, A then B, each waited for in the assignment events, and one reconciler.

| Case | Injection | Method and phase |
|---|---|---|
| C0 | none | baseline; measures T |
| W1 | SIGKILL of the owner | fault file, `before_claim` |
| W2 | SIGKILL of the owner | fault file, `after_claim` |
| W3 | SIGKILL of the claiming worker | harness, 3 s into `spark_pipeline` |
| W4 | SIGKILL of the owner | fault file, `after_pipeline` |
| W5a | SIGKILL of the owner | fault file, `after_accept_commit` |
| W5b | SIGKILL of the owner | fault file, `after_accept` |
| W6 | SIGSTOP of the worker until the takeover, then SIGCONT and SIGTERM | harness, mid-step |
| W7 | SIGSTOP of the whole tree for 90 s, then SIGCONT and SIGTERM | harness, mid-step |
| K1 | `docker compose restart kafka` | harness, mid-step |
| K2 | Kafka stopped 30 s around the submit | harness, before the submit |
| D1 | MySQL stopped 30 s | harness, mid-step |
| D2 | MySQL stopped 30 s while the owner holds | fault file `after_pipeline` (hold) |
| X1 | the job id published again, at its claim and after its success | harness |

## 2. Timing (P2: the defaults of timing.py, no override)

| Lease L | Renewal R | Fence margin M | F | Worker tick | Watchdog t_w | Kill grace G |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 60 s | 10 s | 10 s | last renewal + 50 s | 1 s | 0.5 s | 7 s (5 + 2) |

| Step limits | Attempt | Session S_k | Heartbeat h | Reconciler P | Publication grace g | Confirmation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 120 / 600 / 300 s | 900 s | 15 s | 3 s | 5 s | 30 s | 10 s |

## 3. Deadlines (P3)

D = ceil5(B + 2S): B is the design's latest start of the next run after the deadline's reference,
and 2S is 70.2 s (twice M2's slowest step sum, 35.1 s). `max_lag_s` is 1 s and the drain limit is D.

| Cases | Reference | B | D |
|---|---|---|---|
| C0, W5a, W5b, K1, X1 | submit (C0), injection | 0 | 75 s |
| W1 | injection | S_k + h + 1 = 19 s | 90 s |
| W2, W3, W4, W6 | injection | L + P = 65 s | 140 s |
| W7 | injection | max(L + P, 90 + 2 t_w + G) = 98 s | 170 s |
| K2 | Kafka's return | g + P + 19 = 54 s | 125 s |
| D1, D2 | MySQL's return | L + P = 65 s | 140 s |

A missed injection takes C0's deadline from its submit. The preflight's two C0 jobs took 52.4 and
46.8 s (median 49.6 s). That is above the 40 s assumed but below 70.2 s, so by P3's own rule D is
not re-derived; the margins shrink from 31–35 s to about 20–25 s. Both values come from a host
under memory pressure (section 11). S itself (35.1 s) was measured under host memory pressure too,
so D rests on observations of this host, not on a validated standard: on time and late classify
jobs on this host and nothing more.

## 4. Predictions

The table assumes T = 40 s and restore times of about 20 s; neither has been measured on this clock.
"Finish by" is the latest finish the design predicts, B + T, from the deadline's reference; the
margin is D minus it.

| Case | Claims / accepted | Detection and window | Finish by | Margin |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C0 | 1 / 1 | — | T, 40 s | 35 s |
| W1 | 1 / 1 | standby's `delivered`, 12–19 s | 59 s | 31 s |
| W2, W4 | 2 / 1 | reconciler's `requeued`, 60–65 s | 105 s | 35 s |
| W3, W6 | 2 / 1 | `requeued`, 50–65 s | 105 s | 35 s |
| W7 | 2 / 1 | `requeued`, 50–65 s; the replacement waits for the host lock until 98 s | 138 s | 32 s |
| W5a | 1 / 1 | — ; Q3a `no matching report`, by design | — | — |
| W5b | 1 / 1 | — | — | — |
| K1 | 1 / 1 | — (the attempt goes on) | under T | over 35 s |
| K2 | 1 / 1 | reconciler's `published`, within P of Kafka's return | 94 s | 31 s |
| D1 | 1 / 1 if MySQL is back before F, else 2 / 1 | `renewal_failed`; then `renewed` or `requeued` | 105 s | 35 s |
| D2 | 1 / 1 if MySQL is back before F, else 2 / 1 | `retry` of `accept_result`; then `accepted`, or `failed_after_ack` and `requeued` | 105 s | 35 s |
| X1 | 1 / 1 | both duplicates refused as `succeeded` | T | 35 s |

Expected for E1 on all 28 jobs: Q1 `ok`; `status --check` exits 0; no invariant violation; every
accepted result equals the reference run; no overlapping step intervals. Each of these is checked
per job and reported as found.

**Assumptions and uncertainty.**
- T is unmeasured on the default clock. The preflight's C0 jobs measure it; if T exceeds 2S (70.2 s),
  re-deriving D is the author's option.
- Restore times are unmeasured. From the stop, F comes 40–50 s later; MySQL returns after 30 s plus
  its restore. D1's and D2's branches therefore depend on the restore, and both branches are valid
  outcomes.
- A killed worker's dead group member keeps its session for 15 s, so a restart may take about 20 s
  rather than the estimator's 12 s.
- During K1 and K2, consumers log `consumer_error` and keep polling, with no back-off; the rejoin
  bound of 19 s is assumed to hold.
- X1's first duplicate arrives while its owner runs the job, so it is read only afterwards. Both
  duplicates are therefore refused as `succeeded` (outline 3.1, corrected on 2026-10-24).
- Results are counts per case (k of 2), with no rates.

## 5. Injection success and misses (harness)

- **Fault-file cases** (W1, W2, W4, W5a, W5b, D2): the owner is read from the assignment events,
  and only its fault file is armed (`armed` records `owner_after`).
  - Made: that worker's `fault_injected` at the case's point, after this job's `delivered` or
    `claimed`. For kills, the worker has also exited within 30 s. `t_inj` is the event's `mono`, or
    the MySQL stop for D2.
  - Missed: the other worker claims the job first (a miss at once), or no event comes within 300 s.
    The file is then removed.
- **Mid-step cases** (W3, W6, W7, K1, D1):
  - Made: a claim with `step_started` for `spark_pipeline`, no `step_ended` (named `name`) and the
    step's log file, and the step still running 3 s later.
  - Missed: 300 s without that phase, or the step ended during the 3 s.
- **K2**: the stop precedes the submit. A submit that fails is `job_not_submitted` and stops the
  batch.
- **X1**: made once a claim is seen; the second publication follows the success.
- **A missed job is still followed.** Its latencies are `n/a: injection missed`, and it keeps its
  row as `missed`.

## 6. Stop rules and outcomes

- **The batch stops** when one of these happens; the remaining jobs are recorded as `not_run`, with
  the reason:
  - a job is unfinished at its drain limit (`an unfinished job`);
  - a submit fails;
  - a container's batch peak passes 95% of its limit (provisional P4; 90% is flagged);
  - an error in the harness during a job (`job_error`).

  Quiescence (SIGKILL of the writers), the final snapshot and `down -v` still run.
- **Late:** running at its deadline and succeeded later. It counts as `late` with `deadline_met` no,
  and the later success never changes that.
- **Failed:** out of attempts. Q1 `failed`, Q2 `failed`, `deadline_met` no.
- **Unknown:** each is reported as unknown, never as met or as no overlap:
  - a failed deadline read gives `deadline not observed`, with `deadline_met` unknown;
  - a step without both monotonic times makes the overlap `unknown`;
  - a missing injection time gives `unknown: no injection time`;
  - a missing harness record gives `unrecorded`.
- **Validity (6.1):** a batch that fails it does not count, and its records and outcomes stay. E1
  and E2 findings never change validity.

## 7. Commands (from the repository root of the checkout that ran the plan)

```bash
# 0. Preconditions: the test window is released; nothing of this project runs
docker compose -f docker/compose.yaml ps -a -q                 # must print nothing
uv run --group jobs python -m etf_risk.services others         # other projects' containers: a count
git status --short                                             # clean: the batch records the commit
pmset -g batt | head -1                                        # 'AC Power' (section 12)
ioreg -r -k AppleClamshellState -d 4 | grep '"AppleClamshellState"'   # '= No': the lid is open
uv run --group jobs python -c "import psutil; print(psutil.virtual_memory().available / 2**30)"   # GiB (section 12)

# 1. Live preflight (8.6 of the outline): before any formal batch, kept apart from formal results
uv run --group jobs python -m etf_risk.jobs.harness plan --purpose preflight --seed 1 \
    --jobs C0,W1,W6,W7,K1,K2,D1,D2,C0 --out data/outputs-recovery/preflight/plan-1.json
# Keep the host awake: on AC power with the lid open (section 12); -s works on AC power only
caffeinate -dims uv run --group jobs python -m etf_risk.jobs.harness batch \
    --plan data/outputs-recovery/preflight/plan-1.json --out data/outputs-recovery/preflight/<name>
uv run --group jobs python analysis/collect_recovery_measurements.py \
    --batch data/outputs-recovery/preflight/<name>
# The job tests and the live pipeline tests against both services, outputs kept with the preflight
docker compose -f docker/compose.yaml up -d --wait mysql kafka
uv run --group jobs python -m etf_risk.services ready mysql kafka
ETF_RISK_MYSQL_URL=mysql://root:jobs-test@127.0.0.1:3307 ETF_RISK_KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP=127.0.0.1:9094 \
    uv run --group jobs python -m pytest tests/test_jobs_*.py 2>&1 | tee data/outputs-recovery/preflight/job-tests.txt
ETF_RISK_LIVE_PIPELINE=1 ETF_RISK_MYSQL_URL=mysql://root:jobs-test@127.0.0.1:3307 \
    ETF_RISK_KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP=127.0.0.1:9094 uv run --group jobs python -m pytest tests/test_jobs_live_pipeline.py \
    2>&1 | tee data/outputs-recovery/preflight/live-pipeline.txt
docker compose -f docker/compose.yaml down -v

# 2. Formal batch: only after the author approves Part A; the plan is the preferred draft by default

    --out data/outputs-recovery/formal/plan-<SEED>.json
```

**What is and is not established.**
- **M2's isolated check** validated the containers' memory limits (MySQL 512 MiB, Kafka 640 MiB),
  under host memory pressure and with documented sampling limits.
- **Its 5 GiB and 4.0 GiB figures** were the gates of that check. They were never established as
  requirements for recovery experiments.
- **Its step times** (35.1 s for the calendar-year job) were also measured under host memory
  pressure.
- **Native-process memory** (workers, launchers, the Spark driver and JVM, the reconciler, the
  harness) is unvalidated.

None of these is used here as a validated standard. This draft earlier proposed a 2.5 GiB minimum
before each job; nothing measured ties that figure, or any other, to unchanged recovery behaviour on
this host, so it is withdrawn. Every live run so far had 1.2–1.9 GiB available, swap in use and
memory pressure at warning.

**The protocol, for every batch, preflight or formal:**
1. **AC power throughout.** Checked before the start with `pmset -g batt`, and recorded in every
   host reading. A reading on battery fails the batch for timing.
2. **Lid open throughout.** Recorded (`AppleClamshellState`) in every reading. A closed reading fails
   the batch for timing.
3. **Sleep prevented.** The batch runs under `caffeinate -dims`, whose `-s` holds on AC power only.
   The clock check (1 s) detects any sleep that happens anyway and fails validity, as it did for
   preflight-3.
4. **No competing tests.** The exclusive window; no other containers (counted at the start); no
   other pytest, Spark or job processes (checked before the start).
5. **Memory pressure and swap recorded, never gated.** Available memory, swap in use, the bytes
   swapped in and out, and macOS's pressure level, at the start, before each job and at the end
   (`8c5331d`). Each job gets the swap activity of its window, and the batch its totals.
6. **Controls in the same batch.** C0 jobs measured in the same batch, under the same recorded host
   state: the 28-job plan's two shuffled C0s, plus, as proposed, one C0 at the start and one at the
   end (30 jobs, about 2 minutes more). Each case's times are reported next to these controls, for
   example its overhead over their median, rather than next to any external figure.
7. **Every outcome kept.** A batch that fails conditions 1–3 stays invalid for timing and is never
   relabelled.

**Three kinds of claim.**

| Claim | Made from | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Correctness** (E1): one accepted result per job, no overlapping steps, fencing, Q1 and Q3, accepted results equal to the reference, invariants | any batch whose checks that do not involve time pass: code identity, unchanged inputs, equal fingerprints, complete records. From a batch invalid for timing, they are kept as that batch's correctness observations, labelled as such (preflight-3) | "W3 kept one accepted result and no overlap across a 22-min host sleep" |
| **Recovery times observed on this host** (E2) | only batches that meet conditions 1–4 and pass validity, clock check included; reported with the batch's host record and its controls | "W3: requeued 59.1 s after the kill, finished in 117.1 s; the controls took 45.1 and 50.9 s; pressure 2, 26.5 MiB swapped out during the job" (preflight-4) |
| **Performance claims**: recovery time as a property of the job system, comparable across machines or usable as a prediction | not made from this host | — |

- **Why the line falls there.**
  - Correctness rests on the job table's token guards, fencing and the host lock, which do not
    depend on time or memory: all four preflights kept it, under memory pressure and across a sleep.
  - The observed times on this host depend on its memory state. They are taken with swap in use and
    pressure at warning, so they say how this machine recovered in that recorded state, and the
    controls show how fast it ran a job at the same time.
  - A performance claim would need what this host lacks: validated native-process budgets, and a
    memory state that does not swap.
- **The approved use of this host.** On 2026-10-24 the author approved this host's recorded memory
  state for correctness observations and for recovery times observed under its recorded
  conditions, with the limitations above. Performance claims stay out of scope.
- **Tooling, all implemented:**
  - Conditions 1, 2 and 5: power, lid, memory pressure and swap recorded at every reading
    (`8c5331d`).
  - Condition 6: the harness's default plan puts a C0 control at each end (`5a81bc5`).
  - The collector's verdicts (`5a81bc5`):
    - correctness observations rest on code identity, unchanged inputs, equal fingerprints and
      complete records;
    - recovery times also need the clock check and conditions 1 and 2 at every reading the batch
      needs (start, each job that ran, end);
    - a reading on battery or with the lid closed fails;
    - a missing reading, or one without the value, is unknown, and unknown fails.
  - `injections.csv` gives each job its power, lid, pressure and swap activity.
